claims.text: Adding 1–3 at.% Cu to a Zr-based metallic-glass alloy enhances its glass-forming ability.
Adding Cu reduces the critical cooling rate required for glass formation.
The relevant Cu addition range is 1–3 at.%.
Cu addition modifies the alloy's atomic-scale structure.
Cu addition modifies chemical short-range order in the alloy.
Modification of atomic-scale structure and chemical short-range order causes a reduction in the critical cooling rate.
The reduced critical cooling rate leads to improved glass-forming ability.
Adding 1–3 at.% Cu produces a 20–30% reduction in critical cooling rate relative to the Cu-free baseline alloy.
Cu contents above 5 at.% may promote crystalline-phase formation.
Crystalline-phase formation at Cu contents above 5 at.% may degrade glass-forming ability.
The effect of Cu on glass-forming ability may depend on the specific alloy composition and cooling rate.
Failure to obtain at least a 15% critical-cooling-rate reduction with 1–3 at.% Cu is designated as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The predicted reduction is 20–30%, but the hypothesis is falsified only below 15%; therefore, a measured reduction from 15% to less than 20% would violate the stated quantitative prediction without falsifying the hypothesis.

The experiment specifies only a single cooling rate of 10^4 K/s while claiming to measure the critical cooling rate. Determining a critical rate normally requires varying cooling rate or an equivalent explicitly defined procedure.
